prd.name: BedTerm MVP
prd.overview: An iOS terminal app designed for coding on iPhone. Users SSH into a Mac mini or Linux box and run Claude Code, Codex CLI, or any terminal tool — with a special keys bar that makes Ctrl combinations, arrows, and Escape comfortable on a touchscreen. The product differentiator is the mobile keyboard experience for terminal input, not the SSH feature count.

requirement.name: SSH Connection
requirement.description: Connect to a remote Linux or macOS host over SSH with standard authentication methods.
requirement.rule: User can enter a hostname and port to connect.
User can enter a username for authentication.
User can authenticate with a password.
User can authenticate with an SSH private key.
A valid connection opens the terminal session and displays the remote shell prompt.
A failed connection shows a descriptive error message without crashing.

The TCP socket carrying the SSH session keeps itself alive against idle NAT and firewall timeouts by sending periodic keepalive probes (default idle ~30s). Long pauses without typing do not silently strand the session in a half-open state.

rule.context: TCP connection reset by the remote peer or an intermediate gateway

requirement.rule: The disconnect banner shows a human-readable reason — e.g. "Connection reset by the remote host (network change or idle timeout)" — rather than the raw read(descriptor:pointer:size:) / errno text.

requirement.name: Terminal Display
requirement.description: Full terminal emulation rendering ANSI escape sequences, VT100 control codes, colors, and cursor positioning correctly.
requirement.rule: ANSI color codes (16-color and 256-color) render with correct foreground and background colors.
VT100 cursor movement and positioning work correctly.
Clear screen sequences repaint the terminal viewport correctly.
Running vim or nano displays the editor UI correctly, including status lines and cursor positioning.
Running top or htop displays the process list with live updates.
Long lines wrap correctly within the terminal width.

Every rendered character cell shows the complete glyph: descenders (g, j, p, q, y) are fully visible and no row is vertically clipped, regardless of scroll position, input timing, or row position in the viewport.

requirement.name: Special Keys Toolbar
requirement.description: A slim toolbar pinned above the system keyboard that exposes the keys most essential to terminal use but absent from the iOS keyboard. The toolbar is deliberately minimal — only [ESC], [CTRL], and [TAB] on the leading side, plus the R15 keyboard-dismiss toggle and the R11 direction-pad toggle on the trailing side — to keep the input area light and uncrowded.
requirement.rule: The toolbar displays exactly three keys: [ESC], [CTRL], and [TAB]. No other keys (no arrows, no extras) appear on the toolbar.
Only the app's special-keys toolbar appears above the system keyboard. No additional input-accessory bar from the embedded terminal emulator (or any other source) is stacked above or below it.
The toolbar stays visible when the system keyboard is shown and when it is hidden.
Tapping [ESC] sends the escape key (e.g., to exit insert mode in vim).
The toolbar uses the iOS 26+ Liquid Glass material — translucent, depth-aware, responsive to the content scrolling beneath it — instead of an opaque bar.

The toolbar is a leading-aligned Liquid Glass capsule that hugs its three keys — it is not stretched to full screen width. It shares the bottom row with the R13 compose pill on the trailing side, matching the iOS 26 floating-controls pattern used by Notes (leading multi-action capsule + trailing single-action capsule).

When the system keyboard is visible, the toolbar rides directly above the top edge of the keyboard — moving up with the keyboard as it presents and back down as it dismisses — so the keys stay reachable without a gap between the keyboard and the toolbar.
When the system keyboard is not visible, the toolbar floats above the bottom safe-area inset. The direction pad (R11), when shown, overlays the terminal directly above the toolbar.
The toolbar fits within the available safe area without overlapping the terminal view, the direction pad, or the system keyboard.
Tapping [↑] sends the up arrow key to the terminal (e.g., for shell history). Moved off the toolbar — now handled by the direction pad.
Tapping [↓] sends the down arrow key to the terminal. Moved off the toolbar — now handled by the direction pad.
Tapping [←] sends the left arrow key to the terminal. Moved off the toolbar — now handled by the direction pad.
Tapping [→] sends the right arrow key to the terminal. Moved off the toolbar — now handled by the direction pad.
Tapping [TAB] sends the tab character for autocompletion.

requirement.name: Ctrl Combination Mode
requirement.description: Tapping [CTRL] enters a combination mode where the next key press is sent as a Ctrl+key combination. This avoids the need for multi-touch chording on a touchscreen.
requirement.rule: Tapping [CTRL] highlights the key and enters Ctrl-pending mode.
In Ctrl-pending mode, tapping C sends Ctrl+C (SIGINT).
In Ctrl-pending mode, tapping D sends Ctrl+D (EOF).
In Ctrl-pending mode, tapping Z sends Ctrl+Z (SIGTSTP).
In Ctrl-pending mode, tapping L sends Ctrl+L (clear screen).
In Ctrl-pending mode, tapping A sends Ctrl+A (beginning of line).
In Ctrl-pending mode, tapping E sends Ctrl+E (end of line).
If no key is pressed within a short timeout, Ctrl-pending mode cancels and [CTRL] returns to its normal state.
Tapping [CTRL] again while in pending mode cancels the pending state.

Tapping [CTRL] sends the literal Ctrl key code when tapped twice in quick succession, for programs that need a bare Ctrl press. Deferred — a Unix PTY has no byte for a bare Ctrl press; revisit if real usage demands it.

requirement.name: Basic Terminal UX
requirement.description: Standard terminal app conventions for copy, paste, scrolling, text selection, and dark mode.
requirement.rule: User can select text in the terminal and copy it to the system clipboard.
User can paste text from the system clipboard into the terminal.
User can scroll up and down through terminal history with touch gestures.
Scrolling pauses auto-scroll; when scrolled to bottom, auto-scroll resumes and follows new output.

When the transcript is shorter than the viewport, the active prompt line is anchored to the bottom edge of the terminal viewport (just above the special-keys toolbar) and any empty space sits above it. New output fills upward from the bottom, matching the convention of macOS Terminal, iTerm2, and other iOS terminal apps.
The terminal and app UI use a dark color scheme by default.
Terminal text renders in a monospace font.
Landscape orientation. Dropped from MVP — iPhone target locks to portrait. Revisit if real usage demands it.

requirement.name: Host Key TOFU
requirement.description: Trust-on-first-use host key verification. The first successful connection to a host stores the host's public key fingerprint; subsequent connections compare and warn on mismatch. Added during MVP design as the security baseline for any terminal app.
requirement.rule: On first successful connect, the SHA-256 fingerprint of the remote host key is stored in Keychain, keyed by host:port.
On subsequent connects, the stored fingerprint is compared to the remote host key; a match proceeds silently.
A mismatch shows a full-screen warning with both fingerprints (SHA256:base64) and offers Reject or Trust-new-key (with explicit confirmation).

requirement.name: Local Network Permission
requirement.description: iOS shows a system permission prompt the first time the app sends traffic to a Local Area Network address (RFC1918 IPv4, IPv6 unique-local / link-local, or a `.local` mDNS host). The terminal must handle this prompt gracefully so the first connect to a LAN dev box does not fail before the user can tap Allow. Loopback (`127.0.0.1` / `::1`) and public addresses are unaffected and bypass this flow.
requirement.rule: Before opening an SSH connection to a LAN host (RFC1918 / ULA / link-local / `.local`), the app first triggers the iOS local-network prompt and waits for the user's response.
Connections to loopback or to public (non-LAN) addresses skip the prewarm and proceed directly to SSH.
While the prewarm prompt is on screen, the Connect action shows a "Waiting for local network permission…" state instead of returning an immediate failure.
If the user grants permission during prewarm, the app proceeds to the SSH connect automatically — no second tap on Connect required.

If prewarm completes with permission denied (or a connect to a LAN host fails with a permission-shaped error), the app shows an actionable error: "Local network access is required to reach <host>. Open Settings to enable it."
The denied-error surface includes an "Open Settings" button that deep-links to the app's Settings pane, plus a "Retry" button that re-runs the connect.
Once a connect has succeeded against a LAN host, subsequent connects skip the prewarm wait and proceed directly to SSH unless the user changes permission in Settings.

requirement.name: App Icon
requirement.description: Moved to Design R2 — App Icon. This stub is kept so the MVP requirement numbering and existing references stay stable.
requirement.rule: App icon design and Dark/Tinted variants are tracked under Design R2 — App Icon.

requirement.name: System Appearance

description.p: The app always follows the iOS system appearance — Light when the system is Light, Dark when the system is Dark — for both the SwiftUI chrome and the terminal palette. There is no in-app theme override.

The colour tokens that back this behaviour are defined under Design R1 — Colour Tokens. App-chrome rules below are implemented against those tokens; the terminal palette rules remain deferred until SwiftTerm's TerminalTheme is bridged through the same tokens.

requirement.rule: On launch, the app chrome renders in Light or Dark to match the current iOS system appearance, without any in-app theme picker.
Changing the system appearance while the app is open updates the app chrome without restart.
When the system is in Light mode, the terminal uses a light background with dark foreground text and legible ANSI colour mappings.
When the system is in Dark mode, the terminal uses a dark background with light foreground text and legible ANSI colour mappings.
In both appearances, the special-keys bar, Connect form, error text, and disconnect banner meet contrast standards against their background.

Every app-chrome surface, text, icon, border, and accent colour is sourced from a design-system token in the catalogue with both Light and Dark variants — no literal colour values in code. Switching system appearance changes the rendered colour of every coloured element.

requirement.name: First Launch Onboarding
requirement.description: On first launch, before the Connection form, the app guides the user through a short onboarding that captures (a) what kind of host they will connect to and (b) whether that host is on the same Wi-Fi or remote. The answers tailor the next screen — a setup tutorial for macOS, or an immediate local-network permission request for same-Wi-Fi targets. After completion, onboarding does not appear again unless the user resets it.
requirement.rule: On the very first launch (no prior completion), the app shows the onboarding flow instead of the Connection form.
Once the user has completed onboarding, subsequent launches go directly to the Connection form.
Step 1 asks the user to pick the host kind: "macOS" or "Other (Linux / dev box / VM)".
Step 2 asks where the host lives: "Same Wi-Fi as my phone" or "Remote (over the internet)".

When the user picks macOS, the next screen is a tutorial covering how to enable Remote Login on the Mac and how to find the Mac's IP address. Tutorial content is to be authored — placeholder copy is acceptable for the MVP shell.
When the user picks "Same Wi-Fi", the onboarding immediately triggers the iOS Local Network permission prompt (rather than waiting until the first connect attempt).
When the user picks "Remote", the onboarding does not trigger the Local Network prompt — that permission is unnecessary for public hosts.
After the final onboarding step, the user lands on the Connection form, with the host kind / location choice persisted for future reference.
The user can go back to the previous onboarding step at any point before finishing, without losing the earlier choice.

requirement.name: Direction Pad
requirement.description: A user-invoked 4-way direction pad — styled like a game controller's D-pad — provides arrow input for terminal navigation (shell history, cursor movement, TUI menus). Hidden by default to keep the terminal viewport clear; revealed from a dedicated toggle in the special-keys toolbar (R3, adjacent to the R15 keyboard-dismiss toggle), and dismissed by tapping the centre of the pad. While visible, the pad floats over the terminal output — it does not push the terminal — so showing or hiding it never reflows the shell.
requirement.rule: The special-keys toolbar (R3) exposes a dedicated direction-pad toggle button next to the R15 keyboard-dismiss toggle. Tapping it reveals the direction pad; tapping it again hides it.
The direction pad is hidden when a terminal session opens. It only appears after the user taps the R11 toggle.

When shown, the direction pad floats over the terminal output, anchored just above the special-keys toolbar (R3). The terminal viewport keeps its full size — the pad overlays it rather than pushing it up or resizing the PTY.
Each of the four direction buttons is visibly larger than the keys on the R3 toolbar — sized for confident thumb taps, comparable to a physical game controller's D-pad.
The four directions are arranged in a plus / cross layout (Up on top, Down on bottom, Left on the left, Right on the right) around a central dismiss button.
Tapping Up on the pad sends the up arrow key to the terminal (e.g., for shell history).
Tapping Down on the pad sends the down arrow key to the terminal.
Tapping Left on the pad sends the left arrow key to the terminal.
Tapping Right on the pad sends the right arrow key to the terminal.

Tapping the centre of the pad hides the direction pad and returns the screen to the default toolbar-only state. The centre is visually distinct from the four direction wedges so it reads as a dismiss target, not a fifth direction.

Tapping anywhere outside the direction pad — except on the special-keys toolbar (R3), which keeps responding to its own buttons — hides the pad. Taps on the terminal viewport while the pad is shown are consumed by the dismiss action and do not reach the terminal (no selection, no scroll). The toolbar exception means the user can still send Esc / Ctrl / Tab or hide the keyboard without first dismissing the pad.

When the multiline input composer (R13) opens, the direction pad hides automatically so the composer has the full bottom region. The pad does not reappear when the composer closes — the user must tap the R11 toggle again.
Each direction button shows a clear pressed state (visual depression / highlight) and emits a light haptic on tap. The centre dismiss emits a medium haptic.
The direction pad uses the iOS 26+ Liquid Glass material, visually consistent with the R3 toolbar.
Holding a direction continuously repeats the arrow input at a steady rate. Deferred — discrete taps cover the common cases (history navigation, short cursor moves); revisit if usage demands it.
Previously: the pad was always docked between the terminal output and the toolbar. Superseded — the pad is now opt-in and overlays the terminal rather than occupying its own row.

Previously: the pad had to fit in the safe area without overlapping the terminal. Superseded — overlap with the terminal viewport is now intentional, and the pad never overlaps the toolbar or the system keyboard.

requirement.name: Lookin Debug Inspector
requirement.description: Debug builds of the app expose their live view hierarchy to the Lookin Mac client (lookin.work), so the iOS team can inspect SwiftUI / UIKit layout, layer geometry, and view attributes at runtime without rebuilding. Release builds must not include Lookin at all — neither the framework nor any of its symbols ship to the App Store. This is a developer-tooling requirement, not a user-facing feature.
requirement.rule: Debug builds bundle the Lookin server framework, so a running debug instance is inspectable from the Lookin Mac client.
Release builds (TestFlight / App Store) do not link the Lookin server framework and do not expose any view-inspection endpoint.
With a Debug build running on a device or simulator on the same Wi-Fi network as the Mac, the Lookin Mac app discovers the running app and can attach to it.

After attaching, the Lookin client can browse the full SwiftUI/UIKit view hierarchy — the Connection screen, the Terminal screen, the toolbar, the direction pad, and the embedded terminal view — and read each view's frame, bounds, and key properties.

Lookin's presence does not change any user-visible behaviour, layout, performance, or permission prompts in either Debug or Release builds beyond the standard local-network prompt already covered by R7.

requirement.name: Multiline Input Composer

description.p: A user-invoked composer that lets the user draft a multi-line message off the wire and then send it to the terminal as one block. Default behaviour is unchanged: keystrokes from the system keyboard go straight to the PTY. The composer is opened from a dedicated floating affordance, and exited by sending or by an explicit Cancel control inside the composer.

Closed state — leading 4-key capsule (R3 + R15 toggle) + trailing compose pill, Notes-style. The capsule holds ⎋ ⌃ ⇥ on the leading side and the R15 keyboard-dismiss toggle on the trailing side, separated by a thin divider that marks the toggle as a different kind of action (mode toggle vs. character injection):

Open state — collapsed (single line, default). Trailing pill morphs into a single-row pill that holds the text input, an inline ✕ Cancel, and a small circular ↑ Send all on one row. Height is just enough to hold one line of monospace text plus padding. Future affordances (voice, attach) slot in between the text and the ✕.

Open state — expanded (multi-line). As the user types past one line the container grows to fit the content, up to a maximum of 112pt. Above that maximum the container stops growing and the text scrolls inside it. Layout shifts to corner-anchored controls: ✕ Cancel moves to the top-trailing corner; ↑ Send sits at the bottom-trailing corner; the text occupies the leading column with right padding reserved for the controls.

div.div: surface-level reasons, but the underlying logic here makes more sense I've tried a similar approach before and we should all know that this

requirement.rule: When the composer is not presented, the system keyboard sends keystrokes directly to the PTY (today's behaviour is preserved).

When the composer is not presented, a floating compose pill is anchored on the trailing side of the bottom row, sharing that row with the special-keys toolbar (R3) on the leading side — the iOS 26 Notes-style pairing of a leading multi-action capsule and a trailing single-action capsule. Tapping the pill opens the composer. The pill uses the iOS 26 Liquid Glass capsule style and a compose / pencil glyph; it does not live inside the special-keys toolbar, and R3's three keys ([ESC], [CTRL], [TAB]) are unchanged.
While the composer is presented, the special-keys toolbar (R3) and the floating compose pill are both hidden. The composer occupies the bottom input slot on its own.

An editable multi-line text area sits directly above the system keyboard. It uses a monospace font matching the terminal, supports the standard iOS text-editing affordances (caret movement, selection, copy/paste), and disables autocorrect, autocapitalisation, and smart punctuation so typed bytes survive verbatim.

The composer accepts input in any iOS-supported language and script (English, Simplified / Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Russian, emoji, etc.). The system keyboard's globe key remains active so the user can switch input languages while drafting — the composer must not restrict the keyboard to ASCII-only. UTF-8 bytes from the composed buffer are sent verbatim to the PTY on Send, matching how a paste of the same characters would behave in macOS Terminal.

The composer opens in a collapsed single-row pill: a capsule-shaped container holds the text input on the leading side, then ✕ Cancel, then a small circular ↑ Send on the trailing side, all on one row. The container's height is just enough to hold one line of monospace text plus its padding.

As the buffer wraps past one line, the composer container grows in height to fit the rendered text. Growth is continuous: every additional line adds a line of height until the maximum is reached. The shape transitions from the capsule (collapsed) to a rounded-rect (expanded) once growth begins.

The composer container stops growing at a maximum height of 112pt. Beyond that point the text scrolls vertically inside the container; the caret remains visible while typing (auto-scroll follows the insertion point).

Once the composer has grown past the single-row state, ✕ Cancel moves to the top-trailing corner of the container and ↑ Send sits at the bottom-trailing corner. The text area occupies the leading column with right padding reserved for these corner controls — text never flows under either control.

Future affordances (voice dictation, attachments, mode toggles) slot into the inline row between the text input and ✕ in the collapsed state, and into the trailing column between ✕ and ↑ in the expanded state. Adding chips does not change the overall composer geometry rules above.

A small circular Send button (up-arrow glyph, ~30pt diameter, tinted accent) sits at the trailing edge of the composer container — inline on the row in the collapsed state, anchored to the bottom-trailing corner in the expanded state. Tapping Send writes the entire buffer to the PTY in one operation, clears the buffer, and collapses the container back to the single-row capsule. The composer stays open so the user can keep drafting; only ✕ Cancel closes it. Send is disabled while the buffer is empty.
If the remote terminal has enabled bracketed paste mode (ESC [ ? 2004 h), Send wraps the buffer in ESC [ 200~ … ESC [ 201~ so shells and editors treat it as a paste rather than per-keystroke input.
If bracketed paste is not active, Send writes the buffer raw with \r as the line separator (matching a real Enter press in a TTY).

Send appends a trailing carriage return so the last line of the buffer runs as soon as it reaches the shell — the user does not have to press Enter a second time after tapping Send. For bracketed-paste sends, the trailing return follows the bracketed-paste close marker so the shell first ingests the paste and then executes the final line.
Tapping the ✕ Cancel control (inline in the collapsed state, top-trailing corner in the expanded state) closes the composer and discards its buffer. The buffer is not preserved across opens in MVP.

After ✕ Cancel closes the composer, keyboard focus returns to the terminal so the next keystroke is delivered to the PTY (default passthrough), and the floating compose pill and the special-keys toolbar reappear. The system keyboard stays up across the handoff — only its first responder changes.

Tapping Send does not close the composer. The buffer clears, the container collapses back to the single-row capsule, focus stays in the text input, and the system keyboard stays up so the user can immediately draft and send another message. The composer is closed only by ✕ Cancel.

Opening and closing the composer animate as a continuous shape morph between the floating compose pill and the composer's input bar, using the iOS 26 Liquid Glass container so the two states share one visual identity.

The closed-state KeyBar capsule, the closed-state compose-entry pill, and the open-state composer's collapsed single-row pill all share the same row height. The bottom row therefore never changes height when the composer opens or closes — only its contents rearrange in place.
The morph is strictly horizontal:
Opening: the trailing compose-entry pill stretches leftward, growing into the full-width single-row composer pill; the leading KeyBar capsule simultaneously slides off the leading edge of the screen and fades out.
Closing: the reverse — the composer's single-row pill shrinks rightward back into the compose-entry pill at its trailing slot, and the KeyBar capsule slides back in from the leading edge.
Both animations run on the same eased curve and share one duration, so the leaving and arriving capsules cross-fade through the same row height with no vertical jump.
The XHTML below loops a full open → close cycle to illustrate the motion (this is a preview only — the production curve and duration come from the iOS animation system, not these stylesheet values):
~/projects/bedterm $ ls -la
total 24
drwxr-xr-x 5 you staff 160 May 17 14:02 .
~/projects/bedterm $
⎋ ⌃ ⇥
⌨︎
✏︎
Compose your message… ✕ ↑
The composer is laid out so the terminal view, the composer, and the system keyboard are all visible at once without overlapping the direction pad (R11).

ui_review.finding: The mockup implies continuous height growth from the single-line capsule upward. The implementation jumps from the 44pt collapsed height to an ~80pt floor the moment the buffer wraps past one line (so ✕ at the top-trailing corner and ↑ at the bottom-trailing corner do not overlap), then continues continuously to the 112pt cap. The 44→80pt step animates smoothly via the same height curve, so it reads as fast continuous growth rather than a hard snap, but it is not strictly continuous either.

requirement.name: Voice Input in Composer
requirement.description: Dictation inside the multiline composer (R13) so the user can speak a long prompt — typically for an AI coding assistant like Claude Code or Codex — instead of typing it on a phone keyboard. Voice input is scoped to the composer only; the main terminal continues to use the system keyboard's built-in dictation if the user wants it there. Recognition runs on-device so audio and transcripts never leave the phone.
requirement.rule: Voice input is available only when the R13 composer is presented. The default terminal passthrough is unchanged and does not gain a mic affordance from this requirement.
The composer exposes a microphone control alongside the Send button. Tapping it toggles dictation on and off; the control reflects idle, listening, and unavailable states.
Speech recognition uses Apple's on-device recognizer (`SFSpeechRecognizer` with `requiresOnDeviceRecognition = true`). The app never sends audio or partial transcripts to a network service.
If on-device recognition is not supported for the current device or locale, the mic control is hidden (or shown disabled with an inline reason) rather than falling back to cloud recognition.

First activation requests both Speech Recognition (`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription`) and Microphone (`NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`) permission. If either is denied, the mic control is disabled and a one-time inline hint points the user to Settings.

Recognized text streams into the composer at the caret position as partials arrive; later partials replace the in-progress region so corrections from the recognizer do not leave stale words. Finalized segments are committed as normal editable text.
After dictation stops, the inserted text is fully editable like any other composer content. The user may continue typing, voice again, or send.
Stopping dictation does not send. Send remains an explicit user action (R13.send_button), preserving the composer's "draft off the wire" guarantee.
Dismissing the composer (R13.dismiss_discards) or backgrounding the app stops any in-flight recognition and tears down the audio session.
Recognition uses the device locale. No in-app language picker is provided in this iteration.
The app activates an `AVAudioSession` only for the duration of dictation, using a recording-appropriate category, and deactivates it on stop. No background or lock-screen recording.

requirement.name: Keyboard Dismiss Affordances
requirement.description: A terminal has two equally important modes: typing and reading. Right now the system keyboard claims roughly a third of the screen and there is no way to put it away — long-running build output, man pages, and scrollback history are all clipped. This requirement adds two complementary ways to dismiss the keyboard: a dedicated toggle on the special-keys toolbar (Termius / Blink idiom) and an interactive drag-down on the terminal scrollback (Messages / ChatGPT / Claude idiom). Both leave the rest of the bottom-row affordances intact: KeyBar, ComposePill, and the direction pad remain reachable; the prompt re-anchors to the new bottom edge of the freed viewport.
requirement.rule: The R3 KeyBar capsule includes a fourth key to the right of [⇥]: a keyboard-dismiss toggle. Tapping it when the system keyboard is shown puts the keyboard away; tapping it when the keyboard is hidden brings the keyboard back. The capsule grows to accommodate four keys without changing any other R3 behaviour.

The toggle's icon reflects its current action: a downward keyboard-chevron when the keyboard is visible ("tap to put away"), and an upward keyboard-chevron when the keyboard is hidden ("tap to bring back"). The two states are exact visual mirrors so users read the same affordance both ways.
Tapping the toggle fires a light impact haptic, matching the other KeyBar keys.
VoiceOver announces the toggle as "Hide keyboard, button" when the keyboard is shown and "Show keyboard, button" when the keyboard is hidden. The state change is announced after the toggle fires.

On every supported width, the four-key KeyBar capsule and the trailing R13 ComposePill maintain visible breathing room and never overlap. On narrow widths the dismiss key may be sized smaller than the other three keys (no smaller than a 44pt hit target) to preserve that breathing room. Implemented for iPhone 17 (220pt capsule + 48pt pill on 393pt width); narrow-width adaptation not yet verified on iPhone SE / mini widths.

After the toggle hides the keyboard, the KeyBar, ComposePill, and direction pad (R11) all remain visible — anchored above the bottom safe-area inset per R3.floats_when_keyboard_hidden — so the user can still send [⎋] / [⌃] / [⇥], open the composer, or navigate without summoning the keyboard.

The terminal viewport grows into the space the keyboard vacated, the remote PTY is resized to the new row count, and the active prompt line re-anchors to the new bottom edge per R5.prompt_anchored_bottom. A TUI program already drawing its own UI on the alternate screen continues to fill the new viewport with no visual gap.

Dragging the terminal scrollback downward puts the keyboard away interactively: the top edge of the keyboard tracks the user's finger frame-for-frame, and the KeyBar / ComposePill ride down with it. Code is wired (UIScrollView.keyboardDismissMode = .interactive set on the SwiftTerm view); the gesture cannot be triggered in the simulator because a software keyboard is not presented while the simulator's hardware keyboard is attached. Awaiting validation on a physical device.

A single tap on the terminal viewport while the keyboard is shown does not dismiss the keyboard — that gesture is reserved for cursor positioning, text selection, and TUI mouse mode (vim, htop). The keyboard is dismissed only via the KeyBar toggle and the interactive scroll-down gesture.

While the composer is open, the KeyBar (and therefore the dismiss toggle) is hidden per R13.keybar_hidden_while_open. The composer keeps its own ✕ Cancel and ↑ Send controls; keyboard dismissal during composition is intentionally out of scope to keep focus on the draft.

When a hardware keyboard is connected and the software keyboard is therefore not presented, the dismiss toggle is hidden from the KeyBar (the capsule reverts to its three R3 keys). Re-attaching / detaching the hardware keyboard updates the capsule live.

The toggle path uses only the system keyboard's own present / dismiss animation, which already respects the user's Reduce Motion setting (the system swaps its keyboard transition for an instant cut). No additional decorative motion is layered on top, so the rule is satisfied implicitly. Re-evaluate when the interactive drag path lands.

If the keyboard is in the hidden state, rotating the device or backgrounding/foregrounding the app preserves that state — the keyboard does not auto-present on layout change. Opening a new SSH session starts with the keyboard shown.

requirement.name: Warp-Style Block Mode
requirement.description: A Warp-inspired alternative terminal view where each shell prompt → command → output cycle is captured as a discrete "block" in a vertically scrolling list, with a persistent composer pinned at the bottom of the screen as the sole input surface. Block Mode replaces the inline cursor-and-prompt model with a chat-like UX better suited to a phone — input lives in one place and output is grouped by command. Block Mode is also the primary delivery vehicle for using the Claude Code CLI (`claude`) over SSH from a phone: the composer's multi-line / voice input (R13, R14) feeds long natural-language prompts into the remote `claude` process, and Block view's alt-screen handling keeps `claude`'s interactive TUI rendering correctly. Block Mode is an opt-in view toggle alongside the classic terminal view (R2), not a replacement; the user can switch between them per session.
requirement.rule: A control in the terminal screen toggles between Classic view (R2, inline prompt) and Block view (this requirement). The choice persists per host and across launches.

Each shell prompt → command → output cycle renders as a distinct block in a top-to-bottom scrolling list. A new block begins on every prompt; the previous block is sealed and shows its command, output, exit code, and duration.

Each block displays a header row with the command string, a coloured exit-code chip (green for 0, red for non-zero, neutral for still-running), and elapsed duration. Tapping the header collapses the block's output body.
Each block's output body renders the captured grid rows in the same monospace font and ANSI palette as Classic view, preserving colours, cursor positioning, and wrapping for that block's row range.

In Block view, the system keyboard's keystrokes route to the composer at the bottom of the screen — not to the PTY. The composer flushes its buffer to the PTY only when the user taps Send or presses Return inside it. This supersedes R13.default_passthrough while Block view is active.
The composer is pinned to the bottom of the screen above the R3 toolbar (and above the keyboard when shown), always visible, never scrolled with the block list.

rule.context: block view, previous command still running

requirement.rule: The user can begin typing the next command in the composer while the previous block's command is still producing output. Composer state is independent of PTY echo until Send.

The terminal parser recognises OSC 133 shell-integration sequences (`A` prompt start, `B` command start, `C` output start, `D;<exit>` command end) and emits a block-boundary event on each, used by Block view to delimit blocks.

On first successful connect to a host, the app offers to install an OSC 133 shell-integration snippet for the remote user's detected shell (zsh, bash, fish) by appending to the appropriate rc file. The user can accept, decline, or "ask again later"; the choice is remembered per host.

If the remote shell has not been instrumented with OSC 133, Block view falls back to a single rolling block that contains all output until the user opens a new session. No heuristic prompt detection is attempted in MVP.

When the remote application enters alt-screen mode (vim, less, htop, fzf, ssh password prompts), Block view automatically collapses into a single fullscreen Classic-style grid and routes keystrokes directly to the PTY. On exit from alt-screen (`CSI ?1049l`), the view restores to Block mode and the alt-screen session is recorded as one block.

The app caps in-memory block output: the most recent N blocks (target: 50) retain full output; older blocks retain only their command, exit code, duration, and an output byte count. Reopening an old block re-renders from a compressed copy on disk if available, otherwise shows a "truncated" placeholder.

Each block exposes a one-tap "Copy output" action that copies the block's full output (or full command + output) to the system clipboard. R5.copy continues to apply for arbitrary text selection within a block.

"Claude support" in BedTerm means first-class support for the Claude Code CLI (`claude`) running as a remote process over SSH, not calling the Anthropic API from the app. BedTerm never holds an Anthropic API key, never makes network calls to `api.anthropic.com`, and never sends terminal contents to any AI service. All AI capability is whatever the user has installed on the remote host.

When the foreground process on the remote PTY is detected as `claude` (via OSC 133 command capture, or via a recognisable banner / title sequence emitted by Claude Code), the active block is tagged as a Claude session and rendered with a distinct accent so the user can tell at a glance that they are talking to Claude, not the shell.

Because Claude Code's interactive TUI uses alt-screen, R15.alt_screen_collapse applies: Block view collapses to a single fullscreen grid for the duration of the Claude session and restores to Block mode on exit. The whole session is captured as one Claude-tagged block in the history.

The R13 composer (and its R14 voice input) is the recommended input path for sending long natural-language prompts to `claude`. Send uses bracketed paste when the remote advertises it so multi-line prompts arrive as a single message rather than per-keystroke input — preserving Claude Code's own input handling.

Block view offers a quick-launch affordance (e.g. a "Start Claude" button surfaced when no Claude session is active) that sends `claude` (or a user-configured launch command) to the PTY. The launch command is editable per host so users with custom invocations (`claude --model …`, `npx @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, etc.) can override it.

BedTerm never prompts for, stores, or transmits an Anthropic API key. Authentication for Claude Code lives entirely on the remote host (its own config / login flow). This is a security guarantee: the app has no AI credentials to leak.

requirement.name: Settings
requirement.description: A dedicated Settings screen, separate from the connection editor, that exposes user-tunable behaviours that today are hard-coded defaults. v1 focuses on connection resilience knobs; the screen is structured so additional categories (appearance, input, advanced) can land later without restructuring.
requirement.rule: A settings affordance in the app's primary navigation (e.g. a gear icon in the connection screen toolbar) opens a Settings screen. The screen presents grouped sections; the first section is "Connection".

The user can choose the TCP keepalive idle interval used by every SSH session. Options include Off, 15s, 30s (default), 60s, 120s. The current selection is persisted across launches and applied to subsequent connections.

A toggle "Reconnect on resume" controls whether the app automatically retries the last session when it returns to the foreground and the session was previously dropped. Default off (so a stranded session shows the existing reconnect banner instead of reconnecting silently).
If the user has never opened Settings, the app behaves as if the defaults above were chosen (keepalive 30s, auto-reconnect off). The user does not have to visit Settings to get sane behaviour.

bug.current: When the multiline composer is opened, the system keyboard is forced into ASCII-only mode. The globe key on the keyboard does nothing useful — input methods for Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Russian, emoji, and any other non-ASCII keyboard installed on the device are unavailable. The user cannot draft a message in their native language inside the composer; only English / ASCII characters can be typed.
bug.expected: The composer keyboard behaves like any normal iOS text field: the globe key cycles through every input keyboard the user has installed (Pinyin, Zhuyin, Kana, Hangul, Russian, emoji, etc.), and characters typed in those keyboards are inserted into the composer buffer as UTF-8 and sent verbatim to the PTY on Send. Autocorrect / autocapitalisation / smart punctuation remain disabled per R13.composer_editor, but language switching is not blocked.
bug.steps: 1. Install at least one non-Latin keyboard on the device (Settings → General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Add New Keyboard…, e.g. Simplified Chinese — Pinyin). 2. Launch the app, connect to any host, and tap the compose pill to open the multiline composer. 3. Tap the globe key on the system keyboard to cycle to the Chinese (or any non-Latin) keyboard. 4. Observe: the keyboard does not switch — it stays on an ASCII-only English layout, and the installed non-Latin keyboards are not reachable from inside the composer.

bug.current: After the keyboard is dismissed (either via the R15 KeyBar toggle or the interactive scroll-down gesture), the KeyBar capsule and ComposePill do not ride down to the bottom safe-area inset. Instead they stay roughly where the top edge of the keyboard was, leaving a large empty band of background between the toolbar row and the actual bottom of the screen. The terminal viewport also stops at this old keyboard edge rather than growing into the freed space — so the bottom ~third of the screen is unused.
bug.expected: When the keyboard hides, the KeyBar capsule, ComposePill, and the terminal viewport's bottom edge all drop to the bottom safe-area inset (just above the home indicator), per R15.keybar_persists_on_dismiss and R15.terminal_reflows_on_dismiss. The empty band below the toolbar must disappear; the prompt re-anchors to the new bottom per R5.prompt_anchored_bottom.
bug.steps: 1. Launch the app and connect to any host. 2. Tap the terminal viewport to bring up the system keyboard. 3. Tap the keyboard-dismiss key on the right side of the KeyBar (or drag the terminal scrollback downward). 4. Observe: the keyboard hides, but the KeyBar and ComposePill stay anchored where the top of the keyboard used to be — there is a large empty area below them.

bug.current: Two stacked toolbars appear above the system keyboard: the app's special-keys toolbar (with arrows and extras still present) on top, and a second grey accessory bar from the embedded terminal emulator below it (showing esc, ctrl, ~, |, /, -, arrows, a touch-mode toggle, and a keyboard-dismiss button).
bug.expected: Only the app's special-keys toolbar is visible above the system keyboard. The terminal emulator's built-in input accessory bar does not appear.
bug.steps: 1. Launch the app and connect to any host. 2. Tap the terminal area to bring up the system keyboard. 3. Observe: two distinct toolbars stack between the terminal and the keyboard.

bug.current: All terminal text renders in the default foreground colour (light grey) regardless of ANSI colour escapes emitted by the remote shell. Directory listings from ls show no directory-blue, no executable-green; even forcing colour with ls --color=always still produces monochrome output. The same shell, viewed through Terminal.app on the host, renders the colours correctly.
bug.expected: ANSI 16-colour, 256-colour, and truecolour escape sequences map to their corresponding foreground / background pixels, matching how macOS Terminal and iTerm2 render the same byte stream.
bug.steps: 1. Connect to a remote host whose shell emits coloured output (e.g. zsh with oh-my-zsh, or any shell with ls --color=always). 2. Run ls --color=always. 3. Observe: every line is the default foreground colour; directory entries are not blue, executables are not green, and so on.

bug.current: On a fresh terminal session, when the remote shell has emitted only a few lines (e.g. Last login: … plus the prompt), those lines render at the top of the terminal viewport and a large empty band fills the space between the prompt and the special-keys toolbar at the bottom. The prompt and cursor sit roughly in the middle of the screen instead of just above the keyboard.
bug.expected: The active prompt line is anchored to the bottom edge of the terminal viewport. When the transcript is shorter than the viewport, the empty space sits above the transcript, not below it. As new output arrives, lines push the existing content upward, matching the behaviour of macOS Terminal, iTerm2, and standard iOS terminal apps.
bug.steps: 1. Launch the app and connect to any SSH host. 2. Observe the freshly opened terminal session — only the login banner line and a prompt are visible. 3. Observe: the prompt sits high in the terminal area with a tall empty band between the prompt and the toolbar. 4. Expected: the prompt sits just above the toolbar with the empty band above the login banner instead.

bug.current:
Touch-scrolling the terminal history does not erase previous paints before drawing new rows. Each scroll frame layers on top of the prior one, producing severe visual corruption:
Every row above the live prompt shows doubled / horizontally-offset glyphs (the same line painted twice, shifted by ~1 character).
After a single swipe-down gesture to reveal scrollback, the entire viewport becomes a vertical-stripe smear of stacked text frames — readable content disappears.
Vertical streaks of stale glyphs persist in the top band even after content scrolls out of view, i.e. that region never fully repaints to the background colour.
Only the bottommost line (the live prompt being typed into) renders cleanly, which points at the scroll-copy / redraw path rather than the per-glyph renderer.
bug.expected:
Scrolling the terminal history repaints the viewport cleanly on every frame:
Each row appears exactly once at its scrolled position; no doubled or offset duplicates.
Areas that scroll out of view are erased to the terminal background colour with no residual glyphs.
Continuous scroll gestures produce a smooth visual translation of the existing content, not an accumulation of overlaid frames.
bug.steps: 1. Open the app and connect to any SSH host so a shell prompt is visible. 2. Run a command that produces enough output to fill the viewport, e.g. ls -la. 3. Observe: rows above the live prompt already render with doubled / offset glyphs. 4. Swipe down inside the terminal view to reveal scrollback history. 5. Observe: the viewport becomes a vertical-stripe smear of stacked text frames; no row is individually legible. 6. Swipe up to scroll content off-screen. 7. Observe: a band of stale glyph streaks remains at the top of the viewport instead of clean background.

bug.current: The app forces Dark appearance at the root, so it renders dark even when the iOS system is in Light mode. The terminal also stays on a dark palette regardless of system setting.
bug.expected: The app and terminal mirror the iOS system appearance — Light in Light, Dark in Dark — with no in-app override. Toggling system appearance while the app is open swaps both the SwiftUI chrome and the terminal palette live.
bug.steps: 1. Set the iOS system appearance to Light (Settings → Display & Brightness → Light). 2. Launch the app. 3. Observe: the app and terminal render in Dark instead of Light. 4. With the app open, switch the system appearance to Dark and back to Light. 5. Observe: the app does not react to the system change.

bug.current: On the first launch, tapping Connect against a LAN host (e.g. `192.168.x.x` or a `.local` host) triggers the iOS local-network permission prompt — but the SSH connect attempt has already started in parallel and fails (timeout / no route) before the user can tap Allow. The user sees a confusing error and must tap Connect a second time after granting permission.
bug.expected: The app should detect that the target is a LAN address, run a permission prewarm to surface the iOS prompt, wait for the user's response, and only then start the SSH handshake. If the user grants permission, the connect proceeds automatically; if denied, an actionable error with "Open Settings" and "Retry" is shown.
bug.steps: 1. Fresh-install the app (or reset its local-network permission in Settings). 2. Open the Connection screen and enter a LAN host (e.g. `192.168.1.10`), port `22`, username, password. 3. Tap Connect. 4. Observe: iOS shows the local-network prompt, and a connection error appears behind it before the user can tap Allow. 5. Tap Allow on the prompt. 6. Observe: the connect does not retry automatically; the user must tap Connect again.

bug.current: After typing input and pressing enter, the current line sometimes renders with the bottom portion of characters clipped off — descenders (g, j, p, q, y) are cut, and the bottom few pixels of every character on the affected row are missing. Other rows render correctly. The issue is intermittent, occurring after some inputs but not others.
bug.expected: Every character cell renders in full — descenders are fully visible, no row is vertically clipped. All rows in the viewport display complete glyphs regardless of scroll position or input timing.
bug.steps: 1. Connect to an SSH host and get a shell prompt. 2. Type several commands and observe the terminal output after each press of enter. 3. Notice: on some lines, the bottom portion of characters is visibly cut off.

bug.current: On a physical device, after the session has been idle for a few minutes (or after the device switches network), the disconnect banner surfaces the raw SwiftNIO error string: Disconnected: read(descriptor:pointer:size:) Connection reset by peer (errno: 54). The text is incomprehensible to a non-developer and gives no hint that the cause is usually network idle / NAT timeout / network change.
bug.expected: When the underlying socket reports ECONNRESET (errno 54), the disconnect banner shows a plain-language reason such as "Connection reset by the remote host (network change or idle timeout)". The raw NIO description is not surfaced to the user.
bug.steps: 1. Connect to an SSH host from a physical device. 2. Lock the device or switch networks; leave the session idle for several minutes. 3. Return to the foreground. 4. Observe: the disconnect banner shows the raw read(descriptor:pointer:size:) errno text.
